title: DHS Moves to End Work Permits for H-1B Spouses, Reviving Trump-Era H-4 EAD Fight
excerpt: The administration has placed H-4 employment-authorization rescission on its regulatory agenda as a long-term action, but no proposed rule has been drafted — current permit holders keep their authorization for now.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security's 2026 regulatory agenda lists a rule titled "Removing H-4 Dependent Spouses From the Classes of Noncitizens Eligible for Employment Authorization" (RIN 1615-AD14), which would roll back the 2015 rule allowing certain H-4 spouses of H-1B workers to work.
  • The item is classified as a "Long-Term Action" with the proposed-rule date marked "To Be Determined." No draft regulation has been published, and USCIS continues to accept and adjudicate Form I-765 applications from H-4 spouses.
  • What to do now: check your EAD expiration date, file renewals on schedule, and speak with an immigration attorney about backup options — the agenda entry changes nothing about your current authorization.
  • The first Trump administration tried the same rescission beginning in 2017, sent a draft to White House review in February 2019, and never published a proposed rule before it was withdrawn in January 2021.

Opening news lead

The Trump administration has put the work permits of H-1B spouses back in its crosshairs. The Department of Homeland Security's 2026 regulatory agenda adds a new rulemaking action titled "Removing H-4 Dependent Spouses From the Classes of Noncitizens Eligible for Employment Authorization," assigned RIN 1615-AD14. According to DHS's abstract, the contemplated rule would remove certain H-4 dependent spouses from the class of noncitizens eligible to apply for employment authorization under 8 C.F.R. § 274a.12(c)(26) — the category created by the Obama-era 2015 final rule that let spouses of H-1B workers on the green-card track obtain Employment Authorization Documents.

The revival is real, but so is the distance between an agenda entry and a rule. The 2026 Unified Agenda classifies the action as a Long-Term Action rather than placing it in the Proposed Rule Stage, and the anticipated date for a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking is listed as "To Be Determined." It is also absent from the administration's Regulatory Plan. As of October 2, 2026, no draft regulation has been prepared, submitted for White House review, or published in the Federal Register.

Context & Background

The 2015 H-4 EAD rule was aimed at a specific population: spouses of H-1B holders who have an approved immigrant petition (Form I-140) or who qualify for H-1B extensions under AC21 — that is, workers already deep in the employment-based green-card queue. Immigration advocacy groups estimate between 90,000 and 100,000 people currently hold active H-4 EADs, many of them highly educated women in technology, health care, research, and finance.

This is not the first time the administration has targeted the program. The first Trump administration announced rescission plans beginning in 2017 under RIN 1615-AC15. That effort went considerably further than the current one: DHS classified it in the Proposed Rule Stage and, on February 20, 2019, submitted a draft proposed rule to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs within the Office of Management and Budget. The public never saw it. The rule sat in White House review until January 25, 2021, when the Biden administration marked the review "Withdrawn." No proposed rule was ever published.

One legal landscape has shifted since that failure. For years the H-4 EAD was challenged in federal court in Save Jobs USA v. Department of Homeland Security, which argued DHS lacked authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act to let H-4 spouses work. On August 2, 2024, the D.C. Circuit rejected that argument and upheld DHS's authority. The Supreme Court denied the challengers' petition for review on October 14, 2025, leaving the ruling intact. The program now rests on stronger legal footing — which, ironically, also simplifies the case for rescinding it: DHS need not argue the 2015 rule was unlawful, only that the agency is making a different policy choice.

Impact & Analysis

If finalized, the rule would stop new applications and could prevent renewals, though the agenda entry does not say whether existing EAD holders would be grandfathered. That question — whether valid permits run to expiration or face earlier termination — will only be answered if an actual proposed rule is published.

"Families shouldn't panic over a proposal that hasn't even been published yet. But they also shouldn't wait to prepare."

— Hector Herrera, Lead Immigration Attorney, Herrera Law Firm

The economic case for rescission will be difficult to build. The first administration's draft was classified as economically significant, requiring DHS to analyze and justify the costs of pulling tens of thousands of employed workers out of the workforce — workers who hold jobs, pay taxes, own businesses, and buy homes. DHS would also have to reckon with reliance interests that are stronger now than in 2019: the program is more than a decade old, and families and employers have made long-term decisions on its foundation.

The political context matters too. The H-4 EAD revival arrives alongside a broader H-1B crackdown — including the $100,000 H-1B petition fee blocked by two federal judges this fall — suggesting the administration is layering multiple pressures on skilled-worker immigration at once.

Diaspora Angle

The rule's weight would fall overwhelmingly on Indian families. Because India faces the longest employment-based green-card backlogs — with H-1B workers routinely waiting a decade or more for permanent residency — Indian households make up the bulk of H-4 EAD holders, and the prospect of losing a second income or a hard-built career lands hardest in a community already rattled by H-1B uncertainty this year.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The signals to watch are procedural, not rhetorical. The first would be RIN 1615-AD14 moving from Long-Term Action into the Proposed Rule Stage with a scheduled NPRM date; the second, submission of a draft to OMB; the third, publication of a proposed regulation in the Federal Register opening a public-comment period. Any final rule would almost certainly face litigation under the Administrative Procedure Act, with opponents arguing DHS has not justified reversing a decade-old policy. Until one of those steps happens, the sensible posture for H-4 EAD holders is attention without alarm: track renewal dates, document green-card progress, and get counsel before making employment decisions the headlines might suggest.
